title: Atherosclerosis
description: Inflammatory disease involving a buildup of lesions in the walls of arteries
wiki_lead:
Atherosclerosis is a pattern of the disease arteriosclerosis, characterized by the development of atheromatous plaques in the walls of arteries. This is a chronic inflammatory disease involving many different cell types and is driven by elevated blood levels of cholesterol, primarily LDL. These lesions lead to narrowing of the arteries.
At the onset, there are usually no symptoms, but if they develop, symptoms generally begin around middle age. In severe cases, it can result in coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease, or kidney disorders, depending on the body part(s) in which the affected arteries are located.
The exact cause of atherosclerosis is unknown and is proposed to be multifactorial. Risk factors include abnormal cholesterol levels, elevated levels of inflammatory biomarkers, high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking (both active and passive smoking), obesity, genetic factors, family history, lifestyle habits, and an unhealthy diet. Plaque is made up of fat, cholesterol, immune cells, calcium, and other substances found in the blood. The narrowing of arteries limits the flow of oxygen-rich blood to parts of the body. Diagnosis is based upon a physical exam, electrocardiogram, and exercise stress test, among others, depending on the affected artery or arteries.
Prevention guidelines include eating a healthy diet, exercising, not smoking, and maintaining a normal body weight. Treatment of established atherosclerotic disease may include medications to lower cholesterol such as statins, blood pressure medication, and anticoagulant therapies to reduce the risk of blood clot formation. As the disease state progresses, more invasive strategies are applied, such as percutaneous coronary intervention, coronary artery bypass graft, or carotid endarterectomy. In some individuals, genetic factors are also implicated in the disease process and cause a strongly increased predisposition to development of atherosclerosis.
Atherosclerosis generally starts when a person is young and worsens with age. Almost all people are affected to some degree by the age of 65. It is the number one cause of death and disability in developed countries. Though it was first described in 1575, there is evidence suggesting that this disease state is genetically inherent in the broader human population, with its origins tracing back to CMAH genetic mutations that may have occurred more than two million years ago during the evolution of hominin ancestors of modern human beings.

Signs and symptoms
Atherosclerosis is typically asymptomatic for decades because the arteries enlarge at all plaque locations; thus, there is no effect on blood flow. Even most plaque ruptures do not produce symptoms until enough narrowing or closure of an artery, due to clots, occurs. Signs and symptoms only happen after severe narrowing or closure impedes blood flow to different organs enough to induce symptoms. grok_lead: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the arteries in which plaquesâcomposed of lipids, cholesterol, calcium, and cellular debrisâaccumulate within the arterial walls, leading to narrowing, hardening, and reduced elasticity of the blood vessels. The term "atherosclerosis" was coined by German pathologist Felix Marchand in 1904 to describe the gruel-like (athero) hardening (sclerosis) of arteries. This progressive condition typically begins in childhood or adolescence and advances over decades, often remaining asymptomatic until significant obstruction occurs, at which point it can impair blood flow and trigger serious complications. As the underlying pathology for many cardiovascular diseases, atherosclerosis is a leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for approximately one-third of all deaths in developed countries as of 2023, primarily through its role in coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral artery disease. The development of atherosclerosis initiates with endothelial injury or dysfunction in the arterial lining, often due to factors such as high blood pressure, turbulent blood flow at arterial branch points, or exposure to toxins like those in cigarette smoke. This damage allows low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol to infiltrate the vessel wall, where it becomes oxidized and triggers an inflammatory response involving monocytes, macrophages, and T-cells, ultimately forming fatty streaks that evolve into fibrous plaques. Inflammation is integral to this process; current scientific consensus holds that excess LDL cholesterol does not cause arterial plaque without inflammation, as no established mechanism supports plaque development independent of inflammation. Advanced plaques may rupture, leading to thrombus formation that acutely blocks arteries and causes events like myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke. Key risk factors for atherosclerosis include modifiable elements such as dyslipidemia (elevated LDL and low HDL cholesterol), hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and sedentary lifestyle, alongside non-modifiable factors like age, male sex (until menopause in women), and genetic predispositions such as familial hypercholesterolemia. Symptoms, when present, depend on the affected arteries: coronary involvement may cause angina or heart attacks, cerebrovascular disease can lead to transient ischemic attacks or strokes, and peripheral artery disease often manifests as leg pain during exertion (claudication). Early detection through lipid profiling, imaging, and risk assessment is crucial, as lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy (e.g., statins), and interventions like angioplasty can mitigate progression and reduce morbidity. Moreover, intensive lifestyle interventions incorporating sustained healthy eatingâsuch as low-fat vegetarian, Mediterranean, or low-carbohydrate dietsâalong with exercise, stress management, and other supportive measures, have demonstrated partial regression of atherosclerotic plaques in clinical trials. In the Lifestyle Heart Trial, a low-fat (10% calories from fat) whole-foods vegetarian diet combined with exercise, stress management, and psychosocial support resulted in a 4.5% relative improvement in coronary artery stenosis after 1 year and 7.9% after 5 years. Similarly, the 2-year DIRECT-Carotid study observed approximately 5% regression in carotid artery vessel wall volume across healthy diets (Mediterranean, low-carbohydrate, or low-fat), primarily driven by weight loss and blood pressure reduction. These observations stem from multimodal interventions where dietary changes and weight loss play central roles. However, recent 2024-2025 evidence indicates that physical activity or exercise alone does not reverse atherosclerosis or cause regression of atherosclerotic plaques. Instead, high levels of physical activity are associated with higher coronary artery calcification (CAC) scores, which may reflect more stable, calcified plaques less prone to rupture, supporting a role in plaque stabilization. Physical activity also improves endothelial function, contributing to overall cardiovascular benefits and potentially slowing atherosclerosis progression, but not reversal. However, full reversal is not always possible, particularly for advanced disease, and requires consistent long-term adherence along with multiple factors; prevention and risk reduction remain primary emphases.
